title: The Boston Tea Party Was Not a Tax Revolt — It Was the Fallout from a London Financial Blowup
dek: The Boston Tea Party was not a tax revolt sparked by heavy burdens on North America, but a self-rescue in which a London financial crisis was passed on to North America through the leverage of the East India Company — one blowup at the imperial center that finally lit the fuse of colonial revolution.
why: A history-of-thought episode that cuts in through a financial-crisis story: it lays out another layer of causation behind the Boston Tea Party, and uses Burke's choices on three fronts — North America, India, France — to force you to weigh anew the old binary of radical versus gradual.
who: For managers choosing between radical reform and gradual improvement, and for Chinese intellectual readers who treat Anglo-American conservatism as a ready-made answer but have never read the original texts.

points.h: The Boston Tea Party was not a tax revolt
points.body: The chain behind the Boston Tea Party lies not in North American tea taxes but in the London financial storm around 1772. Some bankers shorted the East India Company too early, blew up their own positions and fled, dragging down a large batch of small London financial institutions with them; the East India Company's cash flow tightened in turn, with roughly two-thirds of its tea sitting in the warehouses. The solution Britain devised was to divert the tea to North America for clearance sales, and on the surface it looked perfectly balanced: it freed the East India Company and preserved a symbolic tea tax. But what North Americans saw was not the price of tea — it was Londoners once again using the colonies to fill in the pit of their own financial crisis. One act of self-rescue at the imperial center thus became the fuse of North American independence. Burke lived inside exactly such an empire where everything was tangled together: trouble in far-off India had to be resolved by shipping to North America on the other side of the globe.

points.h: Burke was not a thinker but a Commons politician
points.body: Burke was later placed in the history of political thought, but Jiang Yuan reminds us: he was essentially not a cloistered thinker but an Irish-born member of the British House of Commons. As a young man he went to London to study law, then switched to politics, served as secretary to the Marquess of Rockingham, and entered Parliament through a rotten borough controlled by the party leader. The Burke we read today is overwhelmingly not academic works but parliamentary speeches and letters to his Bristol constituency. Two great undertakings marked his career: one was promoting Anglo-American reconciliation, the other was leading the impeachment of Warren Hastings, the first Governor-General of India. Precisely because he was this kind of practical politician, his writing never pushes ideas to extremes and always weighs real difficulties and concessions — this is both why he became a symbol of conservatism for later ages and the filter we should remove when rereading him: he was a man who made judgments, not a prophet who wrote systems.

points.h: An MP is not a loudspeaker for his constituency
points.body: The North American colonies insisted they had no representation in the British Parliament, but Londoners had their own account: the House of Commons operates on virtual representation — an MP does not represent the gains and losses of some district or place, but by independent judgment acts for the whole kingdom, colonies included. Burke's attitude toward this is honestly embodied in the Bristol episode: as the MP elected by the Bristol constituency, he voted in favor of a free-trade bill that damaged Bristol's port monopoly, and wrote that what benefits Britain will ultimately benefit Bristol too. In his view, representation is not carrying the constituency's voice into Parliament, but representing the whole nation through one's own independent judgment as a gentleman. The people of Bristol understood this logic and promptly replaced him at the next election; he then returned to a rotten borough with almost no voters and carried on as an MP. Whether this logic counts as democracy is another question, but it at least challenges an intuition — representative government need not be realized only through one-person-one-vote territorial representation.

points.h: The East India Company's double standard was the real institutional evil
points.body: Burke's impeachment of Hastings was aimed on the surface at one man, but in fact at the double standard of a system. The East India Company was both a company and half a government ruling India: when you ask it to bear governing responsibility for famines and for deaths by the tens of thousands, it says it is only a company and making money for shareholder dividends is enough; but turn around and it has an army, can fight and sign treaties with Indian princes, and take over taxation and justice. Neither a pure company nor a pure government, this state of affairs created a huge arbitrage space — war is individual glory, profit goes to oneself, and the cost of governing failure is left to the Indians and the empire to cover. Adam Smith criticized the East India Company for the same reason. Burke later abandoned mere institutional cleanup and took the dramatic route of impeachment, with the aim of turning the India question into a moral spectacle. Hastings was ultimately found entirely blameless by the House of Lords, but British rule over India turned a corner from then on, shifting from a governance that had blended into Indian society to a clearer, racially segregated form of rule.

Burke is often simplified into an antique who opposed all reform, but conservatism's real point of leverage is not whether to reform but how. Any reform must first examine real difficulties and actual benefits, rather than using a theoretically perfect blueprint to kick over the existing institutional edifice and raise a new building out of thin air. Burke saw society as an organism that grows naturally, not a machine that can be reassembled according to a blueprint, so he would rather patch what good already exists than take risks for abstract ideals. This judgment is mutually consistent with the English experience: England was never a country that raised tall buildings on flat ground — traditions like Magna Carta and the common law were themselves rounds of old-bottle-new-wine reform poured in. But Jiang Yuan also points out its blind spot: Burke's ideal picture always contains an imagination of a tamed, contented lower class, and when ordinary people begin to demand the rights of a human being, this gradualist language can no longer answer.

points.h: From the rights of Englishmen to the rights of man
points.body: The protest logic of the North American colonies in the 1760s was originally entirely English: we are Englishmen, and what we want is rights under the common law and no taxation without representation. But by 1775 and 1776, this English set of liberties was no longer enough to protect them, and the colonies' argument escalated from the rights of Englishmen to the rights of man. The Declaration of Independence no longer said we are British subjects, but instead said all men are created equal and born free. Burke's lifelong strategy of reconciliation with America was always to keep North America within the framework of Englishmen's liberties; he did not believe people could start over from nothing. North America's crossing in ten years from the language of British constitutionalism to the language of natural rights is precisely a lesson for gradualism: gradual reform depends on a window of time, and when the speed and scope of institutional adjustment cannot keep up with external pressure, the same demand turns from a path of improvement into a reason for revolution.

points.h: Gentlemanly mutual trust was the chassis of the Industrial Revolution
points.body: The Industrial Revolution is usually told as the story of Watt and the spinning jenny, but Jiang Yuan adds a condition few mention: the credit infrastructure among strangers. Once the commercial radius expands, you must trust the bill of exchange issued by a London merchant you have never met, trust that a canal fund launched by someone you have never heard of will not cheat you. This mutual trust cannot be maintained by blood ties and local roots; it can only rest on a universal norm — be a decent man, be a gentleman. The emerging industrial and commercial class actively imitated and shared this gentlemanly ethic, and credit gained its endorsement: a Manchester factory owner could sell goods to a distant merchant, and what the other party trusted might not be the goods themselves but that the identity of a gentleman within the system would not be adulterated. This moral consensus amounted to a social operating system outside the formal legal system. Its hint for today is: reforming property rules is easy; cultivating a moral consensus in which strangers can entrust things to one another is far harder.

points.h: The Chinese-speaking world borrowed Burke to bid farewell to revolution
points.body: Burke's fame in Chinese intellectual circles was to a large extent propped up by the farewell-to-revolution current of thought after the 1990s. Jiang Yuan exposes this borrowed relationship: the narrative that improvement is superior to revolution sounds very reasonable, but it is often using Burke's name to vent one's own pent-up feelings. If you actually open Burke, you will see a great deal that looks antiquated and off today — his candid acceptance of a hierarchical society, his expectation of a tamed people, his undisguised faith in elite politics. Burke's own thought is not equal to the Burke shaped in the Chinese-language context. This contrast gives readers a very direct reminder: when we turn a historical figure into the banner of our own position, the question most worth asking is not whether he was right back then, but who we are really talking about when we borrow him.

quotes.text: Burke was not a thinker, not a university professor, not a man who made money by writing books, not a literary man of letters — he was a politician.

You will have a protected, contented, industrious and docile people; you are taught to seek and to acknowledge the happiness found in every condition — the true moral equality of mankind lies in this.

This conservatism does not mean supporting reform, does not mean absolutely refusing reform, but rather that whenever each reform is raised, one must consider its real impact, some real difficulties, and make the improvement that can actually be brought about in reality truly land — rather than saying that because of some theoretical good, I will overturn the existing institutions.
